issues.legal_issue: A mortgage term and its associated conditions constitute a clog on the equity of redemption when, viewed together in their economic and factual setting, they make redemption effectively illusory.
material_facts: The mortgaged property was urban immovable property and the mortgage fixed an exceptionally long period before redemption.
The mortgagor was financially distressed and heavily indebted when the mortgage was made, and the property was his family’s only residence.
Part of the mortgage amount carried interest that was payable only at redemption, causing a substantial accumulation over the long term.
The mortgagee was permitted to reconstruct or improve the property, with the resulting costs chargeable to the mortgagor at redemption.
The long redemption period, deferred interest, reconstruction obligations, and the parties’ financial circumstances operated together to make redemption impracticable.
issues.conclusion: The terms amounted to a clog on the equity of redemption, so the mortgagor could redeem before the stipulated period expired.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, the mortgagor has a continuing statutory right to redeem, and a term that prevents or unduly hampers that right is void; once a mortgage, it must remain a mortgage. A long redemption period alone is not necessarily a clog, but in changing economic conditions an exceptionally long period, considered with the mortgagor’s financial position, the payment terms, the property and other obligations, may make redemption illusory. The court assesses the totality of the circumstances, applying justice, equity and good conscience. The Court relied on Santley v. Wilde, Vernon v. Bethell, G. and C. Kreglinger v. New Patagonia Meat and Cold Storage Company Ltd., and Seth Ganga Dhar v. Shankar Lal; it distinguished Seth Ganga Dhar on its facts and approved the relevant approach in the cited Gujarat decisions, including Khatubai Nathu Sumra v. Rajgo Mulji Nanji and Maganlal Chhotalal Chhatrapati v. Bhalchandra Chhaganlal Shah.

rule.if: mortgage_redemption_proceeding and urban_mortgaged_property and very_long_redemption_term and mortgagor_financially_distressed and interest_deferred_until_redemption and mortgagee_reconstruction_costs_chargeable_to_mortgagor

predicates.mortgage_redemption_proceeding: The mortgagor or a successor sought redemption of a mortgage before the contractually stated redemption time.
predicates.urban_mortgaged_property: The mortgage secured urban immovable property.
predicates.very_long_redemption_term: The mortgage fixed an exceptionally long period before redemption could be sought.
predicates.mortgagor_financially_distressed: The mortgagor was in financial difficulty when the mortgage was made.
predicates.interest_deferred_until_redemption: The mortgage required interest to accumulate and be paid only when the property was redeemed.
predicates.mortgagee_reconstruction_costs_chargeabl: The mortgage allowed the mortgagee to reconstruct or improve the property and required the mortgagor to bear those costs at redemption.

issues.definition: When a redemption proceeding concerns urban property and the stated long term, financial distress, deferred interest and reconstruction costs burdening the mortgagor are all present, the rule treats the mortgage as redeemable before its stated term.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant inducted by a mortgagee into urban property ordinarily cannot remain in possession or claim rent-control protection against the mortgagor after redemption unless the mortgage deed clearly authorizes a tenancy beyond redemption or later tenancy legislation enlarges the tenant’s rights.
material_facts: The tenants were inducted by mortgagees in possession of urban properties.
The mortgage deeds did not clearly and expressly authorize tenancies to continue beyond redemption, and the mortgagees were obliged to return possession when the mortgages ended.
The mortgagors had not concurred in creating tenancies that would bind them after redemption.
The tenants’ rights had not been enlarged by later tenancy legislation after they were inducted.
In one matter, a tenant was inducted after the mortgage period had already expired, which the Court regarded as imprudent and not bona fide management.
issues.conclusion: The tenancies did not bind the mortgagors after redemption, and the tenants were not entitled to rent-control protection against the mortgagors; they had to yield possession.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 76(a) and 111(c) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a mortgagee’s interest as lessor ordinarily ends with the mortgage, and a mortgagee in possession must manage the property prudently. A lease of urban property by a mortgagee does not ordinarily bind the mortgagor after redemption merely because the mortgage deed allows the mortgagee to let the property; the deed must clearly and unequivocally authorize a tenancy extending beyond the mortgage. A tenant may in some circumstances obtain rights through later tenancy legislation, but the Court held that no such enlargement occurred in these cases. Without a continuing landlord-tenant relationship with the mortgagor, the tenants could not claim protection under section 12 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The Court relied on Lalji Purshottam v. Thacker Madhavji Meghaji, All India Film Corporation v. Raja Gyan Nath, Sachalmal Parasram v. Ratnabai, and Om Prakash Garg v. Ganga Sahai; it considered the principles in Mahabir Gope v. Harbans Narain Singh, Harihar Prasad Singh v. Must. of Munshi Nath Prasad, Asa Ram v. Mst. Ram Kali, Dahya Lal v. Rasul Mohammed Abdul Rahim, Prabhu v. Ramdev, and Jadavji Purshottam v. Dhami Navnitbhai Amaratlal in explaining when statutory tenant rights may arise or be enlarged.

rule.if: mortgage_redemption_proceeding and urban_property and mortgagee_inducted_tenant and not deed_expressly_authorized_post_redemption_tenancy and not later_law_enlarged_tenant_rights

predicates.mortgage_redemption_proceeding: A mortgagor or successor sought to recover the property upon redemption of a mortgage.
predicates.urban_property: The leased property was urban immovable property.
predicates.mortgagee_inducted_tenant: The mortgagee in possession, rather than the mortgagor, placed the tenant in possession.
predicates.deed_expressly_authorized_post_redemptio: The mortgage deed clearly and expressly authorized the tenancy to continue after redemption.
predicates.later_law_enlarged_tenant_rights: Tenancy legislation enacted after the tenant entered possession enlarged that tenant’s rights against the mortgagor.

issues.definition: When a mortgage redemption proceeding concerns urban property let to a tenant by the mortgagee, and neither an express post-redemption tenancy nor a later enlargement of tenant rights exists, the tenant must yield possession after redemption.
